questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: The combustion of 0.5 g of a hydrocarbon produced 1.54 g of CO₂ and 0.63 g of H₂O. The molecular mass of the hydrocarbon is 70 g/mol. What is the molecular formula and classification of the hydrocarbon?
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Calculate mass of C and H from combustion products:
• Mass of C in CO₂ = (12/44) × 1.54 = 0.42 g → % C = (0.42/0.5) × 100 = 84%
• Mass of H in H₂O = (2/18) × 0.63 = 0.07 g → % H = (0.07/0.5) × 100 = 14%
Step 2: Determine empirical formula:
• C: 84/12 = 7; H: 14/1 = 14
• Ratio C:H = 7:14 = 1:2
• Empirical formula = CH₂, Empirical mass = 14
Step 3: n = Molecular mass/Empirical mass = 70/14 = 5
• Molecular formula = C₅H₁₀
Step 4: Classification: C₅H₁₀ has formula CₙH₂ₙ → alkene
Conclusion: C₅H₁₀; alkene.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Which of the following alkanes will give the maximum number of monochlorination products (structural isomers only)?
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze each alkane for distinct types of hydrogen atoms (monochlorination gives one product per distinct H type):
• n-pentane (CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃): 3 types of H → 3 products
• isopentane (CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃): 4 types of H → 4 products
• neopentane (C(CH₃)₄): 1 type of H → 1 product
• n-hexane: 3 types of H → 3 products
Step 2: Isopentane has the most distinct types of hydrogen atoms
Conclusion: Isopentane gives maximum (4) monochlorination products.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: The reaction of 2-methyl-2-butene with HBr in the presence of peroxide gives:
options: A mixture of 1-bromo and 2-bromo products in equal amounts
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze the reaction conditions:
• HBr addition to alkene
• Peroxide present
Step 2: Peroxide effect (Kharasch effect):
• In presence of peroxide, HBr adds via free radical mechanism
• This gives anti-Markovnikov product
• However, this applies only to HBr, not HCl or HI
Step 3: BUT - there's an exception:
• 2-methyl-2-butene is a highly substituted alkene (tetrasubstituted double bond)
• Structure: (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₃
• The radical intermediate stability favors the more substituted radical
• Even with peroxide, the product follows Markovnikov orientation due to stability of tertiary radical
Conclusion: 2-bromo-2-methylbutane (Markovnikov product) - the peroxide effect doesn't change the regioselectivity for this highly substituted alkene.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question:
Which of the following is the correct order of stability of the given carbocations?
I: CH₃⁺ (methyl), II: CH₃CH₂⁺ (ethyl), III: (CH₃)₂CH⁺ (isopropyl), IV: CH₂=CH-CH₂⁺ (allyl), V: C₆H₅CH₂⁺ (benzyl)
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze stabilization mechanisms:
• I (Methyl): No α-hydrogens, no stabilization → least stable
• II (Ethyl): 3 α-hydrogens, hyperconjugation
• III (Isopropyl): 6 α-hydrogens, hyperconjugation
• IV (Allyl): Resonance stabilization (2 resonance structures)
• V (Benzyl): Resonance stabilization (4 resonance structures, delocalization over ring)
Step 2: Stability order:
• Resonance > Hyperconjugation
• Benzyl (4 resonance structures) > Allyl (2 resonance structures)
• Isopropyl (6 α-H) > Ethyl (3 α-H) > Methyl (0 α-H)
Step 3: Final order: V > IV > III > II > I
Conclusion: Benzyl > Allyl > Isopropyl > Ethyl > Methyl.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: The hydration of propyne in presence of HgSO₄/H₂SO₄ gives:
options: A mixture of propanal and acetone
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Reaction: Hydration of alkyne (propyne: CH₃-C≡CH)
Step 2: Mechanism:
• Alkyne + H₂O (Hg²⁺ catalyst) → Enol → Keto-enol tautomerism → Ketone
• Markovnikov addition of water to triple bond
• For terminal alkynes: H adds to terminal carbon, OH adds to internal carbon
Step 3: For propyne (CH₃-C≡CH):
• H adds to terminal C (C1)
• OH adds to C2
• Intermediate enol: CH₃-C(OH)=CH₂
• Tautomerizes to: CH₃-CO-CH₃ (acetone)
Step 4: This is different from hydration of ethyne which gives acetaldehyde
Conclusion: Acetone (propanone).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Which of the following alkynes will give a white precipitate with ammoniacal silver nitrate solution (Tollens' reagent)?
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand the test:
• Ammoniacal AgNO₃ (Tollens' reagent) reacts with terminal alkynes
• Terminal alkyne has acidic hydrogen (C≡C-H)
• The acidic H reacts with Ag⁺ to form silver acetylide (white precipitate)
• R-C≡C-H + [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ → R-C≡C-Ag↓ (white) + NH₄⁺ + NH₃
Step 2: Analyze the alkynes:
• 1-butyne (CH₃CH₂C≡CH): Terminal alkyne with acidic H → gives white precipitate ✓
• 2-butyne (CH₃C≡CCH₃): Internal alkyne, no acidic H → no reaction ✗
Conclusion: Only 1-butyne gives white precipitate.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: The reaction of benzene with CH₃Cl in presence of anhydrous AlCl₃ gives toluene. This reaction is known as:
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze the reaction:
• Benzene + CH₃Cl + AlCl₃ → Toluene
• -CH₃ group is being added to benzene ring
• This is substitution of H by alkyl group
Step 2: Identify the reaction type:
• Friedel-Crafts alkylation: Introduction of alkyl group to aromatic ring using alkyl halide + Lewis acid
• Friedel-Crafts acylation: Introduction of acyl group (-COR) using acyl halide
• Wurtz-Fittig: Reaction of aryl halide + alkyl halide + Na → alkylbenzene
• Gattermann-Koch: Formylation of benzene using CO + HCl + AlCl₃/CuCl
Step 3: This is clearly Friedel-Crafts alkylation
Conclusion: Friedel-Crafts alkylation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Which of the following is the most reactive towards electrophilic aromatic substitution (EAS)?
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand EAS reactivity:
• Electron-donating groups (EDG) activate the ring → increase reactivity
• Electron-withdrawing groups (EWG) deactivate the ring → decrease reactivity
Step 2: Analyze substituents:
• Toluene (-CH₃): EDG (+I effect, hyperconjugation) → activates ring
• Benzene: No substituent (reference)
• Chlorobenzene (-Cl): Weak deactivator (-I > +R)
• Nitrobenzene (-NO₂): Strong deactivator (-I and -R effects)
Step 3: Reactivity order:
• Toluene > Benzene > Chlorobenzene > Nitrobenzene
Conclusion: Toluene is most reactive.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: The directive influence of the -NH₂ group in aniline during electrophilic aromatic substitution is:
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand directive effects in EAS:
• Substituents can be classified as o,p-directing or m-directing
• They can also be activating or deactivating
Step 2: Analyze -NH₂ group:
• -NH₂ has lone pair on nitrogen that can donate to ring (+R effect)
• This increases electron density at ortho and para positions
• The +R effect dominates over -I effect
• -NH₂ is strongly activating and o,p-directing
Step 3: Mechanism:
• Lone pair on N delocalizes into ring
• Creates negative charge density at o and p positions
• Electrophile attacks these positions
• Forms most stable sigma complex (Wheland intermediate)
Conclusion: -NH₂ is ortho and para directing (activating).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Benzene does not undergo addition reactions readily because:
options: It has a stable aromatic sextet of electrons that would be destroyed by addition
It contains sp³ hybridized carbon atoms
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand aromatic stability:
• Benzene has 6 π electrons in a cyclic, planar, conjugated system
• Follows Hückel's rule: 4n+2 π electrons (n=1)
• This gives it aromatic stability (resonance energy ~150 kJ/mol)
Step 2: Addition vs Substitution:
• Addition reactions would destroy the aromatic ring structure
• The product would lose aromatic stability
• This is energetically unfavorable
• Substitution reactions preserve the aromatic ring
Step 3: Analyze options:
• A: Incorrect - Being unsaturated doesn't prevent addition (alkenes add readily)
• B: Incorrect - Cyclic structure alone doesn't explain (cyclohexene adds readily)
• C: Correct - Aromatic sextet provides stability that would be lost in addition
• D: Incorrect - Benzene has sp² hybridized carbons, not sp³
Conclusion: Benzene resists addition to preserve its stable aromatic sextet.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Which of the following polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) is known to be the most potent carcinogen?
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand PAH carcinogenicity:
• Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) are formed during incomplete combustion
• Some PAHs are potent carcinogens
• Carcinogenicity depends on structure and metabolic activation
Step 2: Analyze the PAHs:
• Naphthalene: 2 fused rings - weak carcinogen
• Anthracene: 3 linear fused rings - moderate carcinogen
• Phenanthrene: 3 angular fused rings - less carcinogenic than anthracene
• Benzo[a]pyrene: 5 fused rings (bay region structure) - most potent carcinogen
Step 3: Benzo[a]pyrene:
• Found in cigarette smoke, charred food, automobile exhaust
• Metabolized to diol epoxide which binds to DNA
• Causes mutations leading to cancer
• Classified as Group 1 carcinogen by IARC
Conclusion: Benzo[a]pyrene is the most potent carcinogen.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: The reaction of 1-methylcyclohexene with cold dilute alkaline KMnO₄ gives:
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Reaction conditions:
• Cold dilute alkaline KMnO₄ (Baeyer's reagent)
• This is syn dihydroxylation of alkene
• Adds two OH groups to same face of double bond
Step 2: Mechanism:
• Cyclic manganate(V) ester intermediate forms
• Oxygen atoms add to same side (syn addition)
• Hydrolysis gives cis-1,2-diol
Step 3: Product:
• 1-methylcyclohexene → 1-methylcyclohexane-1,2-diol
• Both OH groups on same side (cis)
• This is different from OsO₄ which also gives syn dihydroxylation
Step 4: Hot concentrated KMnO₄ would cleave the double bond (different product)
Conclusion: 1-methylcyclohexane-1,2-diol (cis diol).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Which of the following is the correct order of heat of combustion per CH₂ unit for cycloalkanes?
options: All have the same heat of combustion per CH₂ unit
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand heat of combustion:
• Heat of combustion is the energy released when compound burns completely
• Higher heat of combustion per CH₂ = less stable ring (more strained)
Step 2: Ring strain in cycloalkanes:
• Cyclopropane: 60° bond angles (severe angle strain) - most strained
• Cyclobutane: ~90° bond angles (puckered to reduce strain)
• Cyclopentane: ~108° bond angles (envelope conformation)
• Cyclohexane: ~109.5° bond angles (chair conformation) - least strained
Step 3: Stability order:
• Cyclohexane > Cyclopentane > Cyclobutane > Cyclopropane (most stable to least)
Step 4: Heat of combustion per CH₂ order (inverse of stability):
• Cyclopropane > Cyclobutane > Cyclopentane > Cyclohexane
Conclusion: Cyclopropane has highest heat of combustion per CH₂ due to maximum ring strain.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: The ozonolysis of 2-methyl-2-pentene followed by reductive workup (Zn/H₂O) gives:
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Structure of 2-methyl-2-pentene:
• CH₃-C(CH₃)=CH-CH₂-CH₃
• Double bond between C2 and C3
Step 2: Ozonolysis mechanism:
• O₃ adds across double bond
• Forms ozonide intermediate
• Reductive workup (Zn/H₂O or (CH₃)₂S) cleaves to carbonyl compounds
• Oxidative workup (H₂O₂) would give carboxylic acids
Step 3: Cleavage products:
• C2 side: (CH₃)₂C= → acetone (propanone)
• C3 side: =CH-CH₂-CH₃ → propanal (propionaldehyde)
Step 4: Products are acetone and propanal
Conclusion: Acetone and propanal.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Which of the following is the major product when 2-methyl-1,3-butadiene (isoprene) reacts with HBr at low temperature?
options: A mixture of 1,2- and 1,4-addition products in equal amounts
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Structure of isoprene:
• CH₂=C(CH₃)-CH=CH₂
• Conjugated diene system
Step 2: Addition of HBr to conjugated diene:
• Can give 1,2-addition or 1,4-addition
• 1,2-addition: H adds to C1, Br adds to C2
• 1,4-addition: H adds to C1, Br adds to C4
Step 3: Temperature effect (Kinetic vs Thermodynamic control):
• Low temperature: Kinetic control → 1,2-addition product (faster formation)
• High temperature: Thermodynamic control → 1,4-addition product (more stable, more substituted alkene)
Step 4: At low temperature:
• 1,2-addition is faster
• Product: 3-bromo-2-methyl-1-butene
Conclusion: 3-bromo-2-methyl-1-butene (1,2-addition product) at low temperature.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: The reaction of acetylene with sodium metal in liquid ammonia followed by treatment with methyl iodide gives:
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Reaction sequence:
• Step 1: Acetylene (ethyne) + Na in liq NH₃
• Step 2: Treatment with CH₃I
Step 2: Step 1 - Formation of sodium acetylide:
• HC≡CH + Na → HC≡C⁻Na⁺ + ½H₂
• Terminal alkyne has acidic H (pKa ~25)
• Strong base (NaNH₂) deprotonates terminal alkyne
Step 3: Step 2 - Alkylation:
• HC≡C⁻Na⁺ + CH₃I → HC≡C-CH₃ + NaI
• This is SN2 reaction
• Product is propyne (methylacetylene)
Step 4: This is a method to extend carbon chain of alkynes
Conclusion: Propyne.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question:
Which of the following is the correct order of rate of electrophilic aromatic substitution for the given compounds?
I: Benzene, II: Aniline, III: Nitrobenzene, IV: Phenol
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand EAS rate dependence:
• Rate depends on electron density of aromatic ring
• EDG increase electron density → faster reaction
• EWG decrease electron density → slower reaction
Step 2: Analyze substituents:
• II (Aniline, -NH₂): Strong EDG (+R > -I) → strongly activating
• IV (Phenol, -OH): Strong EDG (+R > -I) → strongly activating, but less than -NH₂
• I (Benzene): No substituent (reference)
• III (Nitrobenzene, -NO₂): Strong EWG (-I and -R) → strongly deactivating
Step 3: Rate order:
• -NH₂ is slightly better electron donor than -OH (N is less electronegative than O)
• Aniline > Phenol > Benzene > Nitrobenzene
Conclusion: II > IV > I > III.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: The toxic effect of benzene on the human body is primarily due to its:
options: Metabolism to toxic epoxides in the liver
Formation of free radicals in blood
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand benzene toxicity:
• Benzene is a known carcinogen (causes leukemia)
• Not directly toxic - requires metabolic activation
Step 2: Metabolic pathway:
• Benzene is metabolized in liver by cytochrome P450 enzymes
• Forms benzene oxide (epoxide intermediate)
• Benzene oxide is highly reactive
• Can bind to proteins and DNA
• Causes mutations and cancer
Step 3: Why other options are incorrect:
• A: Benzene doesn't directly bind DNA - needs metabolism first
• C: Free radical formation is not the primary mechanism
• D: Protein precipitation is not the main toxic mechanism
Conclusion: Benzene toxicity is due to metabolism to toxic epoxides in the liver.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: The Birch reduction of anisole (methoxybenzene) with Na/liq NH₃ gives:
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand Birch reduction:
• Birch reduction: Aromatic ring + Na/liq NH₃ + alcohol → 1,4-cyclohexadiene
• Reduces aromatic ring to diene
• Electron-donating groups (EDG) direct reduction to unsubstituted positions
• Electron-withdrawing groups (EWG) direct reduction to substituted positions
Step 2: Analyze anisole (methoxybenzene):
• -OCH₃ is an EDG (+R effect)
• In Birch reduction, the ring carbons bearing EDG are NOT reduced
• The reduction occurs at the unsubstituted positions
• This gives 1-methoxy-1,4-cyclohexadiene
Step 3: Product structure:
• The methoxy group remains on sp² carbon
• Double bonds are at 1,4-positions relative to substituent
• Product is 1-methoxycyclohexa-1,4-diene
Conclusion: 1-methoxycyclohexa-1,4-diene.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the Wurtz reaction is CORRECT?
options: It is used to prepare alkanes with odd number of carbon atoms
It involves the reaction of alkyl halides with sodium metal to form alkanes with even number of carbon atoms
It can be used to prepare mixed alkanes from two different alkyl halides in good yield
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand Wurtz reaction:
• 2R-X + 2Na → R-R + 2NaX
• Alkyl halide reacts with sodium metal
• Forms alkane with double the carbon atoms
Step 2: Analyze each statement:
• A: Incorrect - Wurtz gives even number of carbons (2 × n), not odd
• B: Correct - Two alkyl halide molecules couple to give alkane with 2n carbons (even)
• C: Incorrect - Mixed Wurtz (two different R-X) gives mixture of R-R, R'-R', and R-R' in poor yield
• D: Incorrect - Wurtz is a coupling/substitution reaction, not addition
Step 3: Limitations of Wurtz reaction:
• Best for symmetrical alkanes (R = R')
• Intramolecular Wurtz can form cyclic alkanes
• Side reactions possible (elimination giving alkenes)
Conclusion: Wurtz reaction forms alkanes with even number of carbon atoms from alkyl halides and sodium.
